items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we wish to prove the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{P}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{Q}]

Content:
How should we proceed?

Content:
Notice that this statement involves two negations [MATH: (\not\equiv).] Also, the antecedent is a more complicated statement than the consequent. This suggests that a contrapositive proof might be fruitful.

Content:
First, recall that the contrapositive of [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.]

Content:
So, the contrapositive form of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\lnot \Big( 4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]

Content:
which is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9).]

Content:
Now, since the implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, instead of proving the original statement, we can prove its contrapositive form.

The contrapositive of the statement is [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a+7 \equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).] We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the definition of congruence modulo [MATH: n.] Recall that [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n \mid (a-b) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad a-b = nk] for some integer [MATH: k.] So, we can reason as follows:

Since [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10),] by the definition of modular congruence, [MATH: 10 \mid (a-b) \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad a-b = 10k] for some integer [MATH: k.]

Now, we express the difference between [MATH: a+7] and [MATH: b+7] through the difference between [MATH: a] and [MATH: b{:}]

Now, notice that [MATH: (a + 7) − (b + 7)|= a + 7 − b − 7; = a − b; = 10k.]

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence in reverse:

Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have [MATH: a+7 \equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).] By proving the contrapositive, we proved the initial statement, as required.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the conditional statement [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and its contrapositive [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P] are logically equivalent. Moreover, it's sometimes easier to prove the contrapositive.

In this case, we need to show that [MATH: \underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3)}_{P} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12)}_{Q}.] The contrapositive of the statement is [MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( 4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},] which is equivalent to [MATH: 4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).] So, we proceed as follows:

The contrapositive of the given statement is [MATH: 4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).] We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the definition of modular congruence. Recall that [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n \mid (a-b) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad a-b = nk] for some integer [MATH: k.] So, we can reason as follows:

By the definition of modular congruence, [MATH: 4a≡4b(mod12)|⇔12∣(4a − 4b); ⇔12∣4(a − b)]

Next, we use the definition of divisibility:

By the definition of divisibility in [MATH: \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: 12 \mid 4(a-b)] means that there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that [MATH: 4(a-b) = 12k.]

Now, we can cancel out the factor of [MATH: 4{:}]

Dividing this equation by [MATH: 4,] we obtain [MATH: a-b = 3k,] which in turn implies [MATH: 3 \mid (a-b).]

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence again:

Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).] By proving the contrapositive, we proved the initial statement, as required.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we wish to prove the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{P}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{Q}]

Content:
How should we proceed?

Content:
Notice that this statement involves two negations [MATH: (\not\equiv).] Also, the antecedent is a more complicated statement than the consequent. This suggests that a contrapositive proof might be fruitful.

Content:
First, recall that the contrapositive of [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.]

Content:
So, the contrapositive form of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\lnot \Big( 4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]

Content:
which is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9).]

Content:
Now, since the implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, instead of proving the original statement, we can prove its contrapositive form.

---

Item 2 — Example: Templates for Proving Modular Congruence by Contrapositive

Example Prompt:
Suppose we wish to construct a direct proof of the following statement using the contrapositive:

> [MATH: 7a \not\equiv 7b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)] if [MATH: a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9).]

To do this, we need to prove the following equivalent proposition.

[MATH: \bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{fvvbbvvnn} } {\phantom{}} \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\bbox[3pt,border:solid black 1pt]{\phantom{vvbbvvnn} } {\phantom{}} \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)]

What are the missing entries?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The contrapositive of [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.]

In this case, we have the statement

[MATH: \underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{P}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{7a \not\equiv 7b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)}_{Q}.]

The contrapositive form of this statement is

[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( 7a \not\equiv 7b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]

which is equivalent to

[MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}7a \equiv 7b} \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a \equiv b} \: (\textrm{mod} \: 9).]

Item 5 — Example: Proving the Addition and Subtraction Properties

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] be integers. Prove, using the contrapositive, that

> if [MATH: a+7 \not\equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10),] then [MATH: a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Sometimes, to prove [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q,] it is easier to prove the contrapositive [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P] that is equivalent to the initial implication.

In this case, we need to show that
[MATH: \underbrace{a+7 \not\equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10)}_{P} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10)}_{Q}.]
The contrapositive of the statement is
[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a+7 \not\equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]
which is equivalent to
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a+7 \equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).]
So, we proceed as follows:

> The contrapositive of the statement is
> [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a+7 \equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).]
> We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the definition of congruence modulo [MATH: n.] Recall that
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n)
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
n \mid (a-b)
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
a-b = nk]
for some integer [MATH: k.] So, we can reason as follows:

> Since [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10),] by the definition of modular congruence,
> [MATH: 10 \mid (a-b)
> \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
> a-b = 10k]
> for some integer [MATH: k.]

Now, we express the difference between [MATH: a+7] and [MATH: b+7] through the difference between [MATH: a] and [MATH: b{:}]

> Now, notice that
> [MATH: (a + 7) − (b + 7)|= a + 7 − b − 7; = a − b; = 10k.]

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence in reverse:

> Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have
> [MATH: a+7 \equiv b+7 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).]
> By proving the contrapositive, we proved the initial statement, as required.

Item 8 — Example: Proving the Multiplication and Division Properties

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] be integers. Prove that if [MATH: a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3),] then [MATH: 4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the conditional statement [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and its contrapositive [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P] are logically equivalent. Moreover, it's sometimes easier to prove the contrapositive.

In this case, we need to show that
[MATH: \underbrace{a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3)}_{P} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12)}_{Q}.]
The contrapositive of the statement is
[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( 4a \not\equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{\lnot \Big( a \not\equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3) \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]
which is equivalent to
[MATH: 4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).]
So, we proceed as follows:

> The contrapositive of the given statement is
> [MATH: 4a \equiv 4b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 12) \quad\Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).]
> We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

We start by using the definition of modular congruence. Recall that
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n)
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
n \mid (a-b)
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
a-b = nk]
for some integer [MATH: k.] So, we can reason as follows:

> By the definition of modular congruence,
> [MATH: 4a≡4b(mod12)|⇔12∣(4a − 4b); ⇔12∣4(a − b)]

Next, we use the definition of divisibility:

> By the definition of divisibility in [MATH: \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: 12 \mid 4(a-b)] means that there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that
> [MATH: 4(a-b) = 12k.]

Now, we can cancel out the factor of [MATH: 4{:}]

> Dividing this equation by [MATH: 4,] we obtain
> [MATH: a-b = 3k,]
> which in turn implies
> [MATH: 3 \mid (a-b).]

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence again:

> Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have
> [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 3).]
> By proving the contrapositive, we proved the initial statement, as required.
